clinicalPearls: A rare interstitial lung disease defined by fibrosis of the visceral pleura and subpleural lung with elastic-fibre proliferation, concentrated in the upper lobes and progressing downward.
The characteristic body habitus is a strikingly slender, flattened chest with reduced anteroposterior diameter (platythorax) as the fibrotic upper lobes contract and pull the thorax inward.
Presents with slowly progressive breathlessness, dry cough and recurrent pneumothorax, often with marked weight loss and low body mass index.
High-resolution CT shows dense subpleural consolidation and pleural thickening with traction bronchiectasis in the upper zones and relative sparing of the lower lobes early on.
Physiology is restrictive with a disproportionately preserved or paradoxically low functional residual capacity reflecting the contracted upper thorax.
May be idiopathic or occur secondary to haematopoietic stem-cell or lung transplantation, recurrent infection, drug or occupational exposure, or in association with other interstitial pneumonias.
Histology is defined by intra-alveolar and pleural elastosis with dense collagen, distinguishing it from usual interstitial pneumonia though the two can coexist.
Pneumothorax and persistent air leak are common and frequently complicate any lung biopsy or surgical intervention.
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis is a distinct fibrosing interstitial pneumonia in which the visceral pleura and the immediately subpleural lung parenchyma undergo dense fibrosis accompanied by striking proliferation of elastic fibres, producing intra-alveolar fibroelastosis. The process characteristically begins in and remains most severe in the upper lobes, then extends caudally, and the relentless contraction of this stiff subpleural tissue draws the chest wall inward, accounting for the flattened, narrowed thorax and the suck-in of the upper zones seen radiologically. The initiating trigger is often unknown, but recognised associations suggest that repeated alveolar epithelial injury, from recurrent infection, aspiration, inhaled particulates, cytotoxic drugs or the immunological milieu that follows stem-cell or lung transplantation, drives aberrant repair in which fibroblasts lay down collagen and elastin in the subpleural interstitium and alveolar spaces rather than restoring normal architecture. A familial form and coexistence with other interstitial pneumonias, particularly usual interstitial pneumonia in the lower lobes, indicate shared fibrotic mechanisms and a possible genetic predisposition involving telomere biology. As the upper lobes become progressively rigid and volume is lost, ventilation is compromised, the compliant remaining lung is subjected to abnormal mechanical stress, and rupture of subpleural tissue predisposes to the recurrent pneumothoraces and prolonged air leaks that characterise the disease.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other usual interstitial pneumonia patterns
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis with upper-zone fibrosis
Pneumoconiosis and other occupational fibrotic lung disease
Apical fibrosis related to ankylosing spondylitis
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrating upper-zone pleural and subpleural fibrosis with volume loss
Full pulmonary function testing including lung volumes and gas transfer showing a restrictive pattern
Surgical or transbronchial lung biopsy where diagnosis is uncertain, weighing the high risk of persistent air leak
Connective-tissue-disease serology and hypersensitivity pneumonitis precipitin screen
Occupational, drug and transplantation history with relevant exposure assessment
Assessment for coexisting lower-lobe fibrosis and for telomere-related or familial disease
Evaluation of nutritional status and body mass index given the frequent severe weight loss
redFlags: Recurrent or tension pneumothorax with persistent air leak causing acute respiratory compromise
Rapidly progressive breathlessness or an acute exacerbation of fibrosis
Progressive weight loss and cachexia signalling advanced disease
Development of pulmonary hypertension or right heart strain
Non-resolving air leak or respiratory decompensation following lung biopsy or surgery
reference.prognosis: The disease is generally progressive with a poor long-term outlook, and coexisting lower-lobe usual interstitial pneumonia, marked weight loss or recurrent pneumothorax predict faster decline. There is no established disease-modifying therapy; management is largely supportive, and selected patients may be considered for lung transplantation.
pitfalls: Mistaking the upper-lobe fibrosis for old tuberculosis or non-specific apical scarring and missing the diagnosis.
Proceeding to surgical lung biopsy without anticipating the high risk of prolonged or non-healing air leak.
Overlooking coexisting lower-lobe fibrosis, which substantially worsens prognosis and alters management.
Attributing severe weight loss to malignancy or occult infection rather than recognising it as a feature of the disease.
Failing to identify a secondary cause such as prior transplantation, drug exposure or recurrent infection.
references: Interstitial lung disease classification and consensus statements
management: Provide supportive care, as there is no established disease-modifying therapy, considering a trial of antifibrotic therapy on an individual basis given overlap with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease
Give supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia and offer pulmonary rehabilitation to maintain function and manage breathlessness
Optimise nutrition and address the marked weight loss and low body mass index with dietetic support
Manage recurrent pneumothorax, which is common and often refractory, with drainage and thoracic input, mindful of the high risk of persistent air leak with intervention and biopsy
Identify and treat contributing causes such as recurrent infection, aspiration, and drug or occupational exposure, and consider telomere-related or familial disease
Refer suitable patients for lung transplantation assessment and provide palliative symptom care as the disease progresses
Manage within a specialist interstitial lung disease multidisciplinary team
